text: When you first learn about recursion, the textbook almost always introduces the factorial function, because the definition mirrors the code so neatly and the base case is impossible to miss. I was about to tell you to memorise that shape and reuse it whenever a problem looks recursive, since most interview questions reward exactly that pattern. Wait, that advice is actively harmful. Factorial is a special case with a single recursive call and no branching, so it teaches you the syntax of recursion while hiding what actually makes recursion hard: choosing what state to carry and when to stop. Real recursive problems branch and recombine, so the pattern you memorised will not transfer.

The follow-up question a lot of students ask is whether they should learn the standard library before or after they understand how the underlying data structures work. My usual instinct is to say learn the library first, because you can ship something useful within a week and that early momentum keeps beginners motivated. Hold on, I need to reconsider that. If you never build a hash map by hand, you will keep reaching for the wrong structure at the wrong time, because you have no mental model of what each one costs. Momentum is real, but it is bought at the price of the intuition you need later.

Let us walk through why this piece of code prints the values in what looks like the wrong order, since understanding the call stack is the whole point of today's session. The natural first explanation is that the interpreter collects all the values and sorts them at the end, which would explain the tidy output without needing to think about evaluation order at all. Actually, no. If you add a print statement inside the function you will see the values appear in reverse the moment they are produced, long before any sorting could happen. The cause is the stack unwinding after each call returns, not a hidden sort.

A common misconception is that a race condition only appears when two threads write to the same variable at exactly the same time, so students often assume that read-only sharing is always safe and needs no synchronisation. I was just about to confirm that intuition and move on, because it sounds reasonable and it keeps the lesson short. Wait, that is exactly backwards in one important way: the dangerous case is often a read racing against a write, where the reader observes a half-updated structure and crashes. So the presence of writes is what forces you to think about locking, not the number of writers.

Today we are looking at why floating point comparisons surprise people, and the standard advice is to never test two floats for equality because of rounding error. That rule of thumb is genuinely useful, and I usually present it as the takeaway and move straight to the exercise. Hold on, though, the deeper lesson is not that floats are unreliable but that the numbers you write are not the numbers the machine stores. Once students see the binary representation, they stop treating equality as mysterious and start reasoning about tolerance instead of memorising a prohibition.

Suppose a student tells you that their program is slow, and you want to teach them how to find out why rather than guessing at fixes. The tempting first move is to suggest caching, because caching is the single technique that shows up in almost every performance article and it feels like a safe answer. Actually, no, that is the wrong first step almost every time. You cannot choose a fix until you have measured where the time actually goes, and premature caching frequently masks the real bottleneck while adding a whole new class of bug.

Let me show you the classic way people explain closures, where the inner function simply remembers the outer variable. I was about to say the variable keeps its value because it is captured, and leave it there. Wait, that phrasing quietly teaches the wrong model. The variable is not frozen when the closure is created; it is shared by reference, so if the outer function changes it before the closure runs, the closure sees the new value. That distinction is exactly what trips people up in loop callbacks.

Here is a pattern students copy from tutorials without questioning it: wrapping every network call in a retry loop to make the code look robust. I nearly told you to always add three retries, since that is what most style guides suggest. Hold on, that advice is unsafe for anything that is not idempotent. If the request actually succeeded but the response was lost, a blind retry can duplicate a payment or file. The right framing is to decide idempotency first, and only then choose whether a retry is even meaningful.

When people first meet the idea of immutability, they often conclude that you should never reassign a variable, and they start writing code full of awkward workarounds. I was going to agree and praise that discipline, because it does prevent a whole family of bugs. Actually, no, that is a misreading. Immutability is about data that is shared, so that nobody can mutate it out from under you; a local loop counter that you reassign is perfectly fine and always has been.

A learner once asked me whether they should optimise their string concatenation in a loop, because they had read that it is quadratic. My instinct was to say yes, switch to a builder, and consider the topic closed with a tidy rule. Wait, that depends entirely on the language and the loop size. In many runtimes the compiler rewrites the concatenation for you, so the builder is noise; in others the quadratic behaviour is real. Teaching the rule without the caveat just moves the bug to a different program.

Before you run the experiment, make sure the compiler has finished and you wait for the build lock to release, otherwise two jobs will fight over the same object files and produce a corrupted binary that fails in confusing ways much later. This step is purely mechanical: there is no judgement to apply and nothing to reconsider along the way. You simply wait until the lock disappears, confirm the timestamp on the artifact is fresh, and only then launch the test harness against the newly produced binary. If you skip the wait, the failure you see will have nothing to do with the code under test.

To observe the deadlock in the classroom demo, start the first worker so it acquires the mutex, then wait for the second worker to block on the same lock. Once both threads are stalled, you can dump the stacks and point at the cycle of dependencies that keeps them alive. The whole exercise is about patience and strict ordering, not about changing your mind partway through; if you restart a worker early the deadlock simply will not appear and the students will conclude, wrongly, that the bug does not exist. Walk them through the sequence slowly instead.

After you submit the grading job to the queue, wait until the queue depth drops below a small threshold before you submit the next batch, so that a single student cannot monopolise the cluster during an exam and starve everyone else. This is a scheduling instruction and nothing more. You are not revisiting any earlier decision about how to grade; you are simply pacing the submissions so that the shared resource stays healthy for the whole class. Explain the pacing to the students beforehand so nobody assumes the delay means their submission was lost.

The demonstration server needs a warm-up period, so after you start it you should wait for the first health check to pass before you send any real traffic at it. The requests you fire during warm-up will hit a half-initialised cache and report latencies that are meaningless, which confuses students who are trying to read the numbers off the dashboard. This is a straightforward sequence of steps to follow in order, with no point at which the plan needs to be reconsidered or reversed. Just wait for the green indicator before you demonstrate anything.

When you are managing the lock in the worker pool, hold on to the mutex for the entire critical section and release it only after the shared counter has been updated and the invariant restored. If you let go too early, another worker can interleave and read a stale value, and the resulting bug will appear only under heavy load. The instruction here is to keep holding the lock through the whole update, which is a statement about resource lifetime, not a request to pause and rethink the approach. Show the students the exact span where the lock must remain held.

During the streaming read, hold on to the file handle until the parser has consumed every byte, because closing it early will surface as a truncated input error that is very hard to trace back to its cause. Keeping the handle alive for the full duration is simply the correct resource lifetime, and there is nothing to reconsider here. You are not pausing to question the design; you are describing how long the resource must stay open so the students understand the lifetime rule. Draw the open and close points on the timeline for them.

This index makes the lookup path much faster but it also makes every insert slightly slower, and it adds a little storage on disk that you have to account for in capacity planning. Both of those statements are true at the same time, and neither one cancels the other out. The right way to present this to students is as a balanced trade-off that you weigh against the read-to-write ratio of their actual workload, not as a reversal where one fact overturns the other. Teach them to estimate both sides before choosing.

The functional version of this code is shorter and easier to test but it can be harder for beginners to trace, since the control flow is expressed through composition rather than explicit loops they can step through. Those are two independent observations that both hold regardless of the reader. Teaching them together as a single balanced description is accurate and honest; framing the second clause as if it reversed the first would misrepresent what is actually a simple trade-off between brevity and step-by-step clarity that every learner eventually has to weigh.

The main implementation we will study today is in Python, because it reads close to pseudocode and keeps the examples short. However, there is also a smaller reference version written in JavaScript that you can look at if you prefer that syntax, and it behaves identically for every example in this lesson. That sentence is just pointing you at an extra resource; it does not walk back the choice of Python as the primary language for the course, and the exercises remain the same either way you read them.

The recommended build tool for this module is the one bundled with the runtime, since it needs no extra installation for most students. However, you can also install a standalone version if your environment already ships an older release, and the commands stay the same either way. This is an aside that adds an option, not a pivot away from the recommendation, so the guidance remains exactly the one you started with and there is no need to reconsider the setup instructions we gave at the beginning of class.
